newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pope brings a little hope to gloomy Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Pope brings a little hope to gloomy Sarajevo.

text.p: Pope John Paul's historic weekend visit to Bosnia brought a glimmer of hope to battle-scarred Sarajevo after a gloomy year of political tensions and poverty.
For two days, nationalist propaganda was overtaken by Papal appeals for reconciliation and tolerance.
Workers spruced up dirty city streets and pilgrims were able to travel across ethnic boundaries to attend an open-air mass in Sarajevo.
"Bosnia was together again," the daily Oslobodjenje wrote on Monday.
The Pope's message of solidarity bouyed many Sarajevans, who had little to cheer about this winter.
More than a year after the war ended, refugees are still barred from returning to their homes and officials use their police forces police to maintain division among rival ethnic communities.
A new inter-ethnic government meets but its Serb, Croat and Moslem represenatives cannot agree on any major issue.

Reconstruction, hampered by political paralysis in Bosnia and economic troubles in the West, has moved slowly. Thousands of pensioners still queue up at soup kitchens and at least half the work force in Bosnia is unemployed.
The city lost gas heating this month because Moslem and Serb politicians cannot agree how to pay an outstanding debt to a Russian gas company.
While foreign troops, diplomats and aid workers have descended on the country to build the peace, most talented young Bosnians have given up on their country and emigrated.
In the weeks leading up to the Pope's visit, Bosnian Moslem leaders opened a public discussion questioning whether it was still realistic to pursue a multi-ethnic ideal.
The Pope's outspoken support for restoring Bosnia's cultural diversity came as a welcome relief to moderates struggling to keep the goal of co-existence alive.
Bosnian Cardinal Vinko Puljic, who has spoken out against religious intolerance, told reporters on Monday the church would work to carry out the Pope's words.
"The Pope spoke about things that need to be done. And the church will understand that seriously as the message from its leader to work on the path of reconciliation," Puljic said.
Many feared that the Pope's visit might not be enough to undo the firmly entrenched nationalism whipped up over the past five years.
"But how long will the light created by his visit last?" asked a commentary in Oslobodjenje. "Shall we listen to the message that the urge to revenge should give way to forgiveness?"
There was no warm welcome for the Pope in Bosnian Serb territory, where many Orthodox Christian Serbs resent the Vatican for recognising Bosnian statehood.
Hardline Serb nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik, a member of the collective presidency, told the Pope that he supported appeals for reconciliation.
But Krajisnik drew a different interpretation of reconciliation than his Moslem rivals.
He said in a speech that reconciliation was preferable to talk of pursuing war crime suspects indicted by a U.N. tribunal.
"A political witch-hunt against alleged war criminals must be replaced by a policy of reconciliation and forgiveness..." he said.
Krajisnik and other Serb leaders have refused to hand over indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb president who still wields influence in Serb territory.
